## Summary


**What this article covers:** How the Life360 driver report works, what driving behaviors it tracks, how to read the data, and how to use it to have real conversations about safe driving with your teen.


### Who It’s For


-


Parents of teen drivers trying to feel less anxious behind the wheel (of life)


-


Families with new drivers who want data over drama


-


Life360 members curious about what's actually inside the driver report


-


Anyone wondering how to turn driving alerts into productive conversations


### Key Takeaways


-


Life360 tracks top speed, phone usage, hard braking, and rapid acceleration on every detected drive.


-


A drive must be at least half a mile long and reach speeds over 15 mph to be logged.


-


Free members get a Weekly Family Driving Summary; Gold and Platinum members unlock Individual Driver Reports with deeper per-trip data.


-


Hard braking is flagged when your teen slows down 8 mph in a single second. Speeding is flagged at sustained speeds over 80 mph for at least 30 seconds.


-


Phone usage detection works by sensing the phone's physical movement while the car is in motion.


-


Turning off location sharing does not stop driving history from being recorded.


-


The data is a starting point for honest conversations with your teen about their driving habits.


Your teen just got their license. You’re proud, terrified, and doing that thing where you casually check your phone every five minutes even though you promised yourself you wouldn’t. The[Life360 driver report](https://www.life360.com/driving-safety) gives you something to work with besides your imagination. It compiles data from your teen’s trips, including how fast they went, how often they used the phone mid-drive, or whether they braked like someone who learned on a demolition derby track. Here is how it all works and what to do with the information.


#### Data over drama for your new driver.


Life360’s driver report tracks top speed, phone usage, and hard braking, so conversations start with facts instead of guesswork.


[See Driving Safety](https://life360.onelink.me/JqZQ?af_web_dp=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.life360.com%2Ffeatures%2Fdriving-safety&pid=web&c=blog_driver-report&deep_link_value=open)


## How Life360 Detects a Drive


Life360 automatically detects a drive when a few conditions align. Your teen's phone needs location services to be active, the app has to be allowed to run in the background, and the battery needs to be above 10%. A trip must cover at least half a mile and reach a speed of over 15 mph to qualify as a drive in the app.


If those conditions are not met, Life360 labels it a Trip instead of a Drive, which means it will not generate driving behavior data. Good to know if you are wondering why a short school run did not show up in the weekly numbers.


One question parents often ask: does turning off location sharing also turn off driving history? The answer is no. Turning off location sharing in the app will not prevent the Weekly Family Driving Summary from showing your teen's driving history for the week. The driving data is stored separately from the location data.


## What the Life360 Driver Report Tracks


The Life360 driver report captures four categories of driving behavior, each defined by a concrete threshold:


-


**Top Speed** is exactly what it sounds like. It’s the highest speed recorded during any trip in the reporting period. If your teen hit 87 mph on the freeway on Tuesday, that number shows up.


-


**Phone usage** is flagged any time the phone is being physically interacted with while the car is moving—texting, opening apps, calling, watching videos, posting, etc. If your teen touches their phone while they’re driving, Life360 detects the motion. It does not read messages or emails, listen to calls, or detect what app was opened, and it won’t flag a hands-free call or Bluetooth connection.


-


**Hard braking** is triggered when the car slows down by about 8 mph or more in a single second. That is an abrupt stop, not a gradual slowdown. It could mean distracted driving, a surprise stop sign, or a little too much confidence in yellow lights.


-


**Rapid acceleration** works on the same scale. It’s triggered by a sudden burst of 8 mph or more in one second. This might be a hard launch off a stoplight or a merge that got a little dramatic.


-


**Speeding** , as a flagged event, is logged when the car exceeds 80 mph for at least 30 consecutive seconds. Life360 considers anything over 80 mph to be high-risk speed territory. It’s not going to flag every highway entrance ramp, just the sustained trips into triple-digit territory.


Together, these five data points give you a picture of how your teen is actually driving when you’re not in the passenger seat.


## Free vs. Paid Driver Reports


Driver reports are different based on what[Life360 membership plan](https://www.life360.com/plans-pricing) you have:


-


**Weekly Family Driving Summary** is available on the free plan. Every Circle member can view a week's worth of driving insights for anyone in their Circle by opening a member's profile. You will see top speed, phone usage, high speed, rapid acceleration, and hard braking for the week. It’s a quick snapshot that resets every seven days.


-


**Individual Driver Reports** are available on Gold and Platinum memberships. These go deeper. You can tap the Driving tab at the bottom of the screen, select a family member, and see their full weekly picture, broken down by category. Total miles, total drives, and each behavior flagged across those trips. The data lets you look at trends across multiple weeks.


If you’re a parent of a new teen driver and relying on the free summary, you’re getting useful information. If you want the per-trip view and ability to look at patterns over time, the Gold or Platinum options are worth the extra cost.


#### Weekly summaries are free. Per-trip detail isn’t.


Gold and Platinum unlock Individual Driver Reports with deeper per-trip data and trends across multiple weeks.

## How to Read the Driver Report


Finding the driver report depends on which version you have access to.


For the free Weekly Family Driving Summary, open the app and go to any Circle member's profile. The summary is right there.


For Individual Driver Reports on Gold and Platinum, tap the Driving tab at the bottom of the screen. Select the family member you want to view. Their full report opens from there, with each behavior category listed.


The phone's sensors generate the data and can occasionally misclassify events. A speed bump hit at the wrong angle could register as hard braking, or a quick lane change might show up as rapid acceleration. The numbers are accurate most of the time, but they are based on sensor data. If an event does not look right, you can check the specific trip and flag a ride as a passenger instead of a driver if the detection got it wrong.


To do that, tap the specific trip in your profile and look for the car icon in the upper-right corner. Tap it to switch between driver and passenger.


## Phone Usage in the Driver Report


Phone use tends to spark the most family conversations. Life360 detects phone use while driving by sensing the phone's physical movement, including orientation changes, screen unlocks, or any interaction that involves touching the device while the car is moving. It won’t flag the phone if the car is stopped at a red light or if it’s answered on a hands-free call or Bluetooth connection. Within two weeks of starting to track driving behavior, 58% of Life360 users reduced their cell phone usage while driving.


## Using Driver Reports to Coach, Not Punish


The driver report gives you data. What you do with it determines whether it becomes useful or just another source of conflict. A one-time speeding flag in an otherwise clean week is a very different conversation from five consecutive weeks of daily phone usage. Life360 lets you see patterns, so you can respond to them rather than react to individual moments.


Some families use the weekly report as a check-in ritual or a quick review. Hey, I noticed a couple of hard braking events this week. What was going on Tuesday? That kind of conversation is much more productive than a general be careful out there as you head out the door.


If your teen is racking up phone usage flags, Life360 doesn’t tell you what they were doing on your phone. It just tells you they were on it. That keeps the conversation focused on the behavior rather than the content, which tends to make things easier to discuss.


## Crash Detection and the Bigger Picture


The driver report is one piece of a larger driving-safety picture within Life360. Crash Detection runs separately and is included on all plans. It monitors for collisions over 25 mph and immediately notifies your Circle and emergency contacts. Gold and Platinum members also get Emergency Dispatch, which means if a crash is detected and there’s no response, Life360 can send help to the exact location.


The driver report and Crash Detection aren’t the same thing, but they work together. Weekly data tells you how your teen is trending. Crash Detection is there when things go wrong.


Drive Detection has to be active for Crash Detection to work. If Drive Detection is turned off in Privacy settings, both features go dark.


## Using Life360's Driving Safety Data


Parents of teen drivers often say the same thing: I trust my kid. I just want to know they got there okay. The driver report is built for that. It’s not about catching anyone doing something wrong but having better information so you can have better conversations.


The data does not lie or exaggerate. Hard braking happened, or it did not. Your phone was in motion while the car was moving, or it was not. There is no spin in either direction, which makes it a genuinely useful tool for parents who want to stay connected without turning every car trip into an anxiety spiral.


Explore Life360's to see how driver reports fit into the full family safety picture.


#### Trends tell you how they drive. Crash Detection has them covered if it goes wrong.

### **Frequently asked questions**


**Why didn’t my teen’s short drive show up in the weekly report?** A trip only counts as a “Drive” if it covers at least half a mile and reaches a speed over 15 mph. Anything shorter or slower gets logged as a “Trip” instead, which doesn’t generate driving behavior data. That’s usually why a quick trip around the block or a short school run doesn’t show up in the weekly numbers.


**If my teen turns off location sharing, does that stop driving data from being tracked?** No. Driving data is stored separately from location data, so turning off location sharing in the app won’t prevent the Weekly Family Driving Summary from reflecting that week’s driving history. Drive Detection needs to be active in Privacy settings for driving behavior, and Crash Detection, to keep working.


**Can the driver report tell what my teen was doing on their phone while driving?** No. Life360 detects phone usage by sensing physical movement, like the phone being touched, unlocked, or changing orientation while the car is moving. It doesn’t read messages, listen to calls, or identify which app was open. It also won’t flag a hands-free call or Bluetooth connection, so the data shows that the phone was in use, not what it was used for.


**What if Life360 misclassifies a passenger ride as a drive?** Sensor-based detection isn’t perfect, and an event like hard braking can occasionally be triggered by something like hitting a speed bump at an odd angle. If a trip was logged incorrectly, open that specific trip in your profile, tap the car icon in the upper-right corner, and switch it from driver to passenger.


**Is Crash Detection the same thing as the driver report?** No, but they work together. The driver report shows trends in driving behavior over time, like speeding or hard braking, while Crash Detection runs separately and monitors for actual collisions over 25 mph, notifying your Circle and, on Gold or Platinum, dispatching emergency help. Both rely on Drive Detection being turned on to function.
